description: The Pragmatic Programmer (20th Anniversary Edition): its philosophy and tips on design (ETC, DRY, orthogonality), tooling, defensive coding, decoupling, concurrency, testing, requirements and teams. For an architect and engineer who wants the habits behind changeable software.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: What does the book mean by "You Have Agency"?
notes.back: If your environment or job is bad, you can act: fix it, or leave. Complaining while waiting for change is the one non-option.
notes.extra: Martin Fowler's line, quoted in the book: "You can change your organization or change your organization."

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: What should you do instead of making an excuse when something fails?
notes.back: Provide options, not lame excuses. Explain what can be done to recover or salvage the situation.
notes.extra: In practice: Before telling a stakeholder "we can't", rehearse it out loud (to a rubber duck). If the excuse sounds lame to you, it will to them.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: What is the core of taking responsibility in the Pragmatic sense?
notes.back: Admit mistakes and ignorance openly, own the outcome you agreed to, and plan for the risks outside your control.
notes.extra: You can refuse responsibility for an impossible situation, but say so up front, not after it fails.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: Broken Windows theory applied to software?
notes.back: One unrepaired flaw (bad design, wrong decision, poor code) signals neglect and invites more. Entropy accelerates once rot is tolerated.
notes.analogy: One broken window left unfixed in a building, and soon the whole building is vandalised.
notes.extra: Tip: Don't live with broken windows. If you can't fix it now, board it up: comment it out, add a 'not implemented' stub, file it.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: How do you "board up" a broken window you can't fix right now?
notes.back: Contain it visibly: replace bad code with a stub or 'not implemented' message, comment it out, or substitute dummy data, so the damage doesn't spread.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: The firefighters-and-carpet story: what lesson does it teach?
notes.back: Even in a crisis, don't add collateral damage. Firefighters rolled out a mat to protect a carpet while the building burned.
notes.extra: When a deadline hits, the temptation is 'it's all broken anyway'. Resist it.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: What is the Stone Soup strategy?
notes.back: When people won't commit resources to an idea, build a small, reasonable piece yourself, show it, and let people join to add to it.
notes.analogy: Soldiers boil a stone in water; curious villagers each add 'just one' ingredient until there's a real soup.
notes.extra: Tip: Be a catalyst for change. Show them a glimpse of the future and they'll rally around it.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: What does the boiled frog warn about?
notes.back: Gradual change goes unnoticed until it's too late: scope creep, slipping quality, a project slowly drifting off target.
notes.analogy: A frog in slowly heating water never notices the moment it should jump out.
notes.extra: Tip: Remember the big picture. Constantly review what's happening around you, not just your own task.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: What makes software "good enough"?
notes.back: It meets users' real needs, as judged by the users themselves, while still meeting legal, safety and maintenance standards. It is not sloppy software.
notes.extra: Tip: Make quality a requirements issue. Let users trade quality against time to market explicitly.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: Why might users prefer imperfect software today over perfect software next year?
notes.back: Early use gives real feedback that improves the eventual solution; a year of polishing in isolation risks building the wrong thing.
notes.extra: Related: know when to stop. Don't spoil a good program with over-embellishment and over-refinement.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: Why manage your knowledge like a financial portfolio?
notes.back: Knowledge is an expiring asset: technologies age and lose value. Regular investment keeps your market value up.
notes.extra: Tip: Invest regularly in your knowledge portfolio.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.text: Knowledge portfolio principles, borrowed from investing: invest {{c1::regularly}} (habit beats amount); {{c2::diversify}} across technologies and domains; manage {{c3::risk}} (mix safe and speculative bets); {{c4::buy low, sell high}} (learn emerging tech early); {{c5::review and rebalance}} periodically.
notes.analogy: A savings plan: small, regular deposits into a spread of funds beat one large lump sum you never revisit.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: Name two concrete knowledge-portfolio goals the book suggests.
notes.back: Learn at least one new programming language every year; read a technical book each month (and non-technical books too).
notes.extra: Also: take classes, join local user groups, experiment with different environments, stay current.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: Why learn a new language even if you won't use it at work?
notes.back: Different languages solve the same problems differently; each one broadens how you think and gets you out of a rut.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: What does "Critically analyze what you read and hear" ask you to check?
notes.back: Ask the Five Whys, who benefits, what the context is, when or where it would work, and why this is a problem at all.
notes.extra: Popularity and search ranking aren't evidence of quality.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: Why does the book say "English is just another programming language"?
notes.back: Communication is a core engineering skill: ideas that aren't communicated well are worthless. Treat prose with the same care as code.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.text: Communicating well: know {{c1::your audience}} (their needs and interests); know {{c2::what you want to say}} (outline it first); choose {{c3::your moment}}; choose {{c4::a style}} that fits the listener; {{c5::listen}} and get feedback; respond to people.
notes.extra: Tip: It's both what you say and the way you say it.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::01 A Pragmatic Philosophy
notes.front: What does "Build documentation in, don't bolt it on" mean?
notes.back: Produce documentation as part of the work (comments, generated API docs, readable code), not as an afterthought.
notes.extra: Comment why something is done, its purpose and goal. The code already shows how; commenting the how violates DRY.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What is the ETC principle?
notes.back: Easier To Change: good design is easier to change than bad design. Every design principle is a special case of it.
notes.extra: In practice: After each change, ask "Did that make the whole system easier or harder to change?"

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: Why do decoupling, single responsibility and good naming all count as ETC?
notes.back: Decoupled concerns change in isolation; single responsibility localises a requirement change to one module; good names make code easier to read and change.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: ETC is a value, not a rule. What should you do when you can't tell which option is easier to change?
notes.back: Pick the option that is easiest to replace later (keep it decoupled), and note the decision so you can review it when you learn more.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What does DRY stand for and actually require?
notes.back: Don't Repeat Yourself: every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system.
notes.analogy: One master copy of a contract: if three edited copies circulate, sooner or later they contradict each other.
notes.extra: DRY is about duplicated knowledge or intent, not about copy-pasted text.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: Is all code duplication a DRY violation?
notes.back: No. Two identical-looking checks that encode different knowledge (e.g. 'age ≥ 0' and 'quantity ≥ 0') are a coincidence, not duplication.
notes.extra: Merging them couples unrelated rules: when one changes, the other breaks.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: How can a comment violate DRY?
notes.back: A comment that restates what the code does duplicates its knowledge; when the code changes the comment goes stale and lies.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: How can a data structure violate DRY? Give the classic example.
notes.back: Storing a derived value next to its inputs, e.g. a Line with start, end and length. Compute length instead.
notes.extra: If you must cache it for performance, hide the cache behind accessors so only the class knows.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: Representational duplication: what is it and how do you reduce it?
notes.back: Your code and an external system (API, database schema) both represent the same structure. Generate one from the other or from a shared spec (e.g. OpenAPI).

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What is inter-developer duplication, and the Pragmatic remedy?
notes.back: Different developers unknowingly implement the same thing. Remedy: strong communication, a shared place for utilities, and code reading.
notes.extra: Tip: Make it easy to reuse. If reuse is hard, people won't.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What does orthogonality mean in software?
notes.back: Two components are orthogonal when changing one doesn't affect the other: independent, decoupled, each with one well-defined purpose.
notes.analogy: A helicopter is non-orthogonal: moving one control changes altitude, heading and speed at once, so the pilot must compensate with the rest.
notes.extra: Tip: Eliminate effects between unrelated things.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What two benefits does orthogonality give?
notes.back: Higher productivity (changes are local, components are reusable and combine well) and lower risk (problems stay isolated, easier to test and replace).

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: A quick test for whether a design is orthogonal?
notes.back: Ask: "If I dramatically change the requirements behind one function, how many modules are affected?" In an orthogonal system the answer is one.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What does "There are no final decisions" warn against?
notes.back: Treating decisions (database, vendor, cloud, framework) as cast in stone. Requirements and technology change, so make critical decisions reversible.
notes.extra: In practice: Hide third-party services and vendors behind your own abstractions so swapping them is a local change.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What does "Forgo following fads" mean for architecture?
notes.back: Nobody knows what the future holds. Don't bet the architecture on today's trend; make it flexible enough to change when the trend does.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What is tracer bullet development?
notes.back: Build a thin, end-to-end, production-quality slice through all layers early, then add flesh to the working skeleton.
notes.analogy: Tracer rounds glow in the dark so gunners see where they hit in real conditions and adjust their aim immediately.
notes.extra: Tip: Use tracer bullets to find the target.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: Why use tracer bullets when requirements are vague?
notes.back: Users see something real early; developers get a structure to work in; integration happens from day one; and you always have something to demo and measure progress against.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: Tracer bullet vs prototype: key difference?
notes.back: Tracer code is kept: lean but complete, part of the final system. Prototype code is thrown away: it exists only to learn something.
notes.analogy: A prototype is the architect's foam model; a tracer bullet is the first floor of the actual building.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What should you prototype?
notes.back: Anything risky, untried or critical: architecture, new functionality, external data formats, third-party tools, performance, User Interface (UI) design.
notes.extra: Tip: Prototype to learn. The value is in the lessons, not the code.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: Which details can a prototype safely ignore?
notes.back: Correctness (dummy data is fine), completeness, robustness (error checking) and style. It's meant to answer one question cheaply.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: Main danger of a coded prototype, and how to avoid it?
notes.back: Stakeholders see it working and demand it be shipped. Make it clear it's disposable, or prototype in tools that can't ship (Post-it notes, whiteboard, scripting language).

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What does "Program close to the problem domain" mean?
notes.back: Use the vocabulary and constructs of the domain in your code, or build a small domain language, so users and code speak the same terms.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: Internal vs external domain language?
notes.back: Internal: written in the host language's own syntax (e.g. an RSpec DSL in Ruby). External: has its own syntax and needs a parser (e.g. YAML config, Cucumber).
notes.extra: Trade-off: internal is cheaper and gets the host language's power; external can be read and edited by non-programmers.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: Why estimate at all?
notes.back: To avoid surprises. Estimates let you judge feasibility and trade-offs before committing.
notes.extra: Tip: Estimate to avoid surprises.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: How do the units of an estimate signal its accuracy?
notes.back: "130 working days" implies day-level precision; "about six months" implies ±1 month. Choose units that match how sure you are.
notes.extra: Book's rule of thumb: 1–15 days → days; 3–6 weeks → weeks; 8–20 weeks → months; longer → think hard before giving a number.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.text: Estimating process: understand {{c1::what's being asked}} (and the needed accuracy); build a {{c2::model}} of the system; break it into {{c3::components}} and give each parameter a value; {{c4::calculate}} the answer; {{c5::keep track}} of your estimates to calibrate.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: What should you say when asked for an estimate on the spot?
notes.back: "I'll get back to you." Off-the-cuff numbers get remembered as commitments.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::02 A Pragmatic Approach
notes.front: How does the book suggest scheduling a project you can't estimate well?
notes.back: Iterate the schedule with the code: estimate per iteration, refine the estimate from the team's real velocity after each one.
notes.extra: Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT) style: give optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values to express a range, not a single number.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: Why keep knowledge in plain text?
notes.back: It outlives the applications that created it, works with every existing tool (diff, grep, version control) and is easy to test.
notes.extra: Binary formats tie knowledge to one program; when it dies, the data dies with it.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: Why use command shells rather than only Graphical User Interface (GUI) tools?
notes.back: Shells let you combine tools, automate sequences and script repeat tasks. GUIs only do what their designers foresaw.
notes.analogy: A GUI is a set menu; the shell is a full kitchen where you can cook anything.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: What does editor fluency mean, and how do you build it?
notes.back: Doing common edits without thinking. Notice when you repeat a clumsy action, look up a better way, and practise it until it's automatic.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: What belongs under version control?
notes.back: Everything: code, docs, build scripts, configuration, memos, even throwaway experiments. It's a project-wide time machine and the backbone of automation.
notes.extra: Tip: Always use version control.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: First rule of debugging?
notes.back: Fix the problem, not the blame. It doesn't matter whose bug it is; it's still your problem.
notes.extra: Then: Don't panic. Think about the cause, not the symptom.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: Why write a failing test before fixing a bug?
notes.back: It proves you've reproduced the bug, confirms the fix works, and keeps the bug from coming back.
notes.extra: Make it reproducible with a single command first.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: What is rubber ducking?
notes.back: Explaining the problem step by step to someone (or something) else. Saying your assumptions aloud often exposes the bug.
notes.analogy: Talking to a rubber duck on your monitor works because explaining forces you to say what you'd silently skip.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: Binary chop in debugging?
notes.back: Halve the search space repeatedly: within a stack trace, a dataset, or a range of releases (git bisect) until you isolate the cause.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: What does "select isn't broken" mean?
notes.back: The bug is almost certainly in your code, not in the OS, compiler or a widely used library. Suspect your own code first.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: What does "Don't assume it, prove it" ask during debugging?
notes.back: When a bug surprises you, one of your 'known' facts is wrong. Prove each assumption in this context, with this data.
notes.extra: Also: Read the damn error message.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: Why learn a text manipulation language?
notes.back: Small scripts in Python, Ruby or similar let you generate code, transform data, write test fixtures and automate chores in minutes.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::03 Basic Tools & Debugging
notes.front: What is an engineering daybook for?
notes.back: A dated log of what you did, learned, sketched and decided. It's more reliable than memory and writing things down helps you think.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: Why are Pragmatic Programmers paranoid, even about their own code?
notes.back: You can't write perfect software. So you code defensively, including against your own mistakes.
notes.extra: "Pragmatic Programmers don't trust themselves, either."

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: What is Design by Contract (DBC)?
notes.back: Specify each routine's rights and duties as preconditions, postconditions and class invariants, and check them, so correctness is explicit.
notes.extra: From Bertrand Meyer and the Eiffel language.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.text: Design by Contract: {{c1::preconditions}} are what must be true for a routine to be called (the caller's duty); {{c2::postconditions}} are what the routine guarantees on completion; {{c3::class invariants}} are always true from the caller's point of view.
notes.analogy: A business contract: the client must pay on time (precondition), the supplier must deliver as specified (postcondition), and both obey the law throughout (invariant).

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: What happens when a contract is violated?
notes.back: A bug has occurred. The program should fail fast, not try to carry on with corrupted state.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: The Design by Contract approach to writing "lazy" code?
notes.back: Be strict about what you accept before you begin, and promise as little as possible in return.
notes.extra: Contrast with Postel's robustness principle ('be liberal in what you accept'), which suits protocols, not internal code.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: What does "Dead programs tell no lies" mean?
notes.back: When something impossible happens, crash early. A dead program normally does far less damage than a crippled one corrupting data.
notes.extra: Tip: Crash early.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: How do Erlang/Elixir apply "crash early" at scale?
notes.back: Let it crash: processes fail fast and a supervisor restarts them in a known-good state, instead of defensive code everywhere.
notes.extra: In practice: Kubernetes liveness probes and restart policies play the supervisor role for containers.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: When should you use an assertion?
notes.back: To check things that 'can never happen'. If you think "that could never happen", add code to check it.
notes.extra: Tip: Use assertions to prevent the impossible. Assertions are not a substitute for real error handling of expected failures.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: Should you turn assertions off in production? Why?
notes.back: Generally no. Testing doesn't find every bug, and production is where the 'impossible' happens. Keep them on except for proven hot spots.
notes.analogy: Turning off assertions in production is like crossing a high wire without a net because you made it across once in practice.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: Why must an assertion have no side effects?
notes.back: If assertions are compiled out, the side effect disappears and the program behaves differently: the check introduces a new bug.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: What does "Finish what you start" mean for resources?
notes.back: The routine or object that allocates a resource should be responsible for deallocating it (files, locks, connections, memory).
notes.extra: Use language support: with, defer, try/finally, destructors.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: Why should every routine allocate shared resources in the same order?
notes.back: To avoid deadlock: if A grabs X then Y while B grabs Y then X, each can wait forever for the other.
notes.extra: Also deallocate in the opposite order of allocation, so you don't orphan resources that reference each other.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: What does "Act locally" mean in resource handling?
notes.back: Keep a resource's scope as small as possible: allocate, use and release it within one routine or block, so ownership is obvious.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: What does "Don't outrun your headlights" warn against?
notes.back: Taking steps bigger than your feedback can cover. Take small steps and check results before going further.
notes.analogy: Driving at night faster than your headlights reach: by the time you see the obstacle, you can't stop.
notes.extra: Tip: Take small steps, always.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::04 Pragmatic Paranoia
notes.front: What does "Avoid fortune-telling" mean for design?
notes.back: Don't design for a far future you can't foresee. Make code replaceable instead of predicting what it will need.
notes.extra: 'Black swans' (rare, unforeseeable events) will make long-range guesses wrong anyway.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: Why does the book say "Decoupled code is easier to change"?
notes.back: Coupling means a change in one place forces changes elsewhere. The fewer the connections, the more local, cheaper and safer each change.
notes.analogy: A bridge needs rigid, coupled parts to stay up; software needs the opposite, because it must keep changing.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: What is a train wreck in code?
notes.back: A chain of calls reaching through objects, like customer.orders.find(id).totals.applyDiscount(). It couples you to every object in the chain.
notes.extra: Tip: Don't chain method calls. Try to have no more than one . when you access something.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: What does "Tell, don't ask" mean?
notes.back: Don't query an object's state, decide for it, then update it. Tell it what you want and let it decide how.
notes.analogy: Tell the restaurant 'one steak, medium rare'; don't walk into the kitchen and flip it yourself.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: Law of Demeter, in the book's practical form?
notes.back: A method should only call methods on: itself, its parameters, objects it creates, and its own direct components. Not on objects those return.
notes.extra: Exception: chaining on things unlikely to change (e.g. the language's standard library) is fine. Pipelines (|>) are not train wrecks.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: Why is global data a form of coupling?
notes.back: Every routine that touches it is coupled to every other one. Reuse and testing require dragging the global along.
notes.extra: Singletons and external resources (databases, files, services) are global data too.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: What should you do when something really must be global?
notes.back: Wrap it in an Application Programming Interface (API). Callers depend on the API, so the underlying data can change without breaking them.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.text: Four strategies for handling events: {{c1::finite state machines}}; the {{c2::observer}} pattern (observers register callbacks); {{c3::publish/subscribe}} (decoupled via channels); and {{c4::reactive programming and streams}} (events as data collections over time).

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: Observer vs publish/subscribe: key difference?
notes.back: In Observer, observers register directly with the subject (coupled, synchronous). In pub/sub, publishers and subscribers only know a channel, so they're decoupled and can be asynchronous.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: When does a finite state machine help with events?
notes.back: When the right response depends on what happened before. It turns tangled conditional logic into an explicit table of states, events and transitions.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: What is transforming programming?
notes.back: Thinking of a program as a pipeline of transformations from input to output, not as a set of objects holding state.
notes.extra: Tip: Programming is about code, but programs are about data.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: Why "Don't hoard state; pass it around"?
notes.back: Data hidden inside objects couples code to those objects. Passing data from one transformation to the next keeps functions simple, testable and composable.
notes.analogy: An assembly line: each station does one step and passes the part on; no station keeps parts in a drawer.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: How does transforming programming handle errors without breaking the pipeline?
notes.back: Wrap values in a result type (ok/error). Each step runs only on ok values and passes errors straight through to the end.
notes.extra: E.g. and_then, Elixir's with, Rust's ?.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: What is the inheritance tax?
notes.back: Inheritance couples a child to its parent, the parent's parent, and every client that uses it. A change high in the tree ripples down unpredictably.
notes.extra: Tip: Don't pay inheritance tax.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: The two reasons people use inheritance, and why both are weak?
notes.back: Code reuse: gives too much coupling for too little reuse. Type modelling: real domains rarely form clean hierarchies, so trees get tangled.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.text: Three alternatives to inheritance: {{c1::interfaces/protocols}} (express polymorphism without shared implementation); {{c2::delegation}} (has-a trumps is-a); {{c3::mixins/traits}} (share functionality without a hierarchy).

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: What does "Delegate to services: has-a trumps is-a" mean?
notes.back: Instead of inheriting behaviour, hold a reference to an object that provides it and call it. You expose only the API you choose.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: Why parameterize your app using external configuration?
notes.back: Values that change after release (credentials, endpoints, thresholds, tax rates) should change without rebuilding code.
notes.extra: In practice: Offer configuration as a service behind an API, so apps can pick up changes dynamically and access is controlled.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::05 Bend, or Break
notes.front: What is Dodo-Code?
notes.back: Code with hard-wired values that can't adapt when its environment changes. Like the dodo, it dies out.
notes.extra: Don't overdo it: making every decision configurable pushes design onto users. Configure what really varies.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::06 Concurrency
notes.front: What is temporal coupling?
notes.back: Code that imposes a sequence that isn't required by the problem: "A must always happen before B" when they could be independent.
notes.extra: Tip: Analyze workflow to improve concurrency.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::06 Concurrency
notes.front: How do you find opportunities for concurrency in a workflow?
notes.back: Draw an activity diagram. Activities with no dependency between them can run in parallel.
notes.analogy: The book's piña colada recipe: you can open the coconut while the blender ice crushes; only pouring must wait for both.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::06 Concurrency
notes.front: What does "Shared state is incorrect state" mean?
notes.back: When several actors read and write the same data without coordination, reads and updates interleave and the state becomes wrong.
notes.analogy: Two waiters see one last slice of pie in the display case and both promise it to their customers.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::06 Concurrency
notes.front: Basic fix for shared-state races, and its main pitfall?
notes.back: Mutual exclusion (semaphores, mutexes, locks) so only one actor updates at a time. Pitfall: forgetting to release, or deadlocks.
notes.extra: Better: put the lock inside the resource, so callers can't forget it; or use transactional resources.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::06 Concurrency
notes.front: What should you suspect when failures occur randomly?
notes.back: A concurrency issue (race condition). Random failures are often concurrency issues.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::06 Concurrency
notes.front: What defines an actor?
notes.back: An independent processor with private state and a mailbox. It processes one message at a time and has no shared state.
notes.extra: Tip: Use actors for concurrency without shared state.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::06 Concurrency
notes.text: Actor model rules: there's {{c1::no single thing in control}}; the only state is {{c2::held inside each actor}}; messages are {{c3::one-way}} (replies are new messages); an actor processes {{c4::one message at a time}}.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::06 Concurrency
notes.front: What is a blackboard system?
notes.back: A shared space where independent agents post facts and react to facts, without knowing about each other.
notes.analogy: Detectives pinning clues on a shared board: anyone can add a clue or act on one, and no one directs the order.
notes.extra: Tip: Use blackboards to coordinate workflow. Modern equivalents: message buses, event streams like Kafka.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::06 Concurrency
notes.front: When does a blackboard beat a fixed workflow?
notes.back: When the order of steps varies or isn't known up front (e.g. a loan application where documents arrive in any order and rules may change).
notes.extra: Trade-off: harder to reason about and debug; needs a common message format and good observability.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: What does "Listen to your inner lizard" mean?
notes.back: Your instincts are pattern-matching on experience. A nagging feeling that code is hard or wrong is data: stop and find out why.
notes.extra: In practice: When it feels like wading through mud, tell yourself 'I'm prototyping', write throwaway code and see what the unease was about.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: How does the book suggest overcoming the fear of the blank page?
notes.back: Start with a deliberately throwaway prototype. Lowering the stakes gets you moving and reveals the design.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: What is programming by coincidence?
notes.back: Code that works by luck: you don't know why it works, so you can't tell why it fails later.
notes.analogy: A soldier who 'safely' crosses a minefield by chance thinks his route is safe and walks it again.
notes.extra: Tip: Don't program by coincidence.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.text: Sources of programming by coincidence: {{c1::accidents of implementation}} (relying on undocumented behaviour); {{c2::accidents of context}} (assuming a GUI, a locale, a fast network); {{c3::implicit assumptions}} (unchecked beliefs about inputs or the environment).

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: How do you program deliberately?
notes.back: Know what you're doing and why; follow a plan; rely only on reliable, documented things; state and test your assumptions; prioritise your effort.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: Why estimate the order of your algorithms?
notes.back: To spot code whose cost explodes with input size (nested loops = O(n²)) before it hits production data.
notes.extra: Tip: Test your estimates. Measure with real data; Big-O ignores constants and small-n effects.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: Is the asymptotically best algorithm always the best choice?
notes.back: No. For small inputs a simple O(n²) algorithm can beat a complex O(n log n) one, and is cheaper to write and debug.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: Why does the book compare software to gardening rather than construction?
notes.back: Software is organic: it needs constant pruning, moving and replanting as conditions change, not a one-time build to a fixed plan.
notes.extra: Tip: Refactor early, refactor often.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: When should you refactor?
notes.back: When you notice duplication, non-orthogonal design, outdated knowledge, changed usage or performance problems. Do it early, before rot spreads.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.text: How to refactor safely: don't {{c1::refactor and add functionality}} at the same time; make sure you have {{c2::good tests}} first; take {{c3::short, deliberate steps}}, running tests after each.
notes.extra: Fowler: refactoring is restructuring code by changing its internal structure without changing its external behaviour.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: Why does the book say "Testing is not about finding bugs"?
notes.back: The main value of tests is the thinking: writing them forces you to design for use, define behaviour and decouple code.
notes.extra: Tip: A test is the first user of your code.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: How does writing tests improve design?
notes.back: Code that's hard to test is usually too coupled. Making it testable forces smaller units, explicit dependencies and clear contracts.
notes.extra: Tip: Design to test.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: What does "Build end-to-end, not top-down or bottom-up" mean?
notes.back: Build small, complete slices of functionality and learn from each, rather than designing everything first or building layers you hope will fit.
notes.extra: The book warns against becoming a TDD (Test-Driven Development) slave: tests don't replace looking at the big picture.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: "Test your software, or your users will": what's the point?
notes.back: Untested code is still tested, by users, in production, at the most expensive time to find bugs.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: What is property-based testing?
notes.back: Specify invariants that must hold for all inputs (e.g. sorting keeps the length) and let the tool generate many random inputs to break them.
notes.extra: Tip: Use property-based tests to validate your assumptions. Tools: Hypothesis (Python), QuickCheck.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: Why does property-based testing find bugs example tests miss?
notes.back: It explores inputs you'd never think to write (empty, huge, odd unicode, edge combinations) and shrinks failures to a minimal case.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.text: Basic security principles: minimize {{c1::attack surface area}}; apply the {{c2::principle of least privilege}}; use {{c3::secure defaults}}; {{c4::encrypt sensitive data}}; maintain {{c5::security updates}}.
notes.extra: Tips: Keep it simple and minimize attack surfaces. Apply security patches quickly.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: Why does code complexity increase security risk?
notes.back: Complex code has more paths and assumptions, so more places for flaws. Simple code is easier to review and leaves fewer gaps for attackers.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: Which attack surfaces does the book highlight?
notes.back: Input data, unauthenticated services, authenticated services (keep authorised users few), output data, and debugging info leaked in errors.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: Why not roll your own cryptography?
notes.back: Crypto is subtle and the smallest error ruins it. Use reputable, well-reviewed libraries and frameworks.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: Why does naming matter so much?
notes.back: Names express intent: readers trust them. A misleading name makes code lie and slows every future reader.
notes.analogy: The Stroop effect: reading the word 'red' printed in blue ink is slow, because the label and reality conflict.
notes.extra: Tip: Name well; rename when needed.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::07 While You Are Coding
notes.front: What should you do when a name no longer fits?
notes.back: Rename it, everywhere, now. If renaming is hard, that difficulty is itself a broken window (ETC violation).

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.front: Why does the book say "No one knows exactly what they want"?
notes.back: Requirements aren't lying around to be gathered; they're buried under assumptions, misconceptions and politics, and must be discovered together.
notes.extra: Tip: Programmers help people understand what they want.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.front: How are requirements actually found?
notes.back: In a feedback loop: build something small, show it, learn from the reaction, and adjust.
notes.extra: Tip: Requirements are learned in a feedback loop.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.front: What does "Work with a user to think like a user" mean?
notes.back: Sit with users and do or watch their work to learn how the system is really used. Interviews alone miss the reality.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.front: What does "Policy is metadata" mean?
notes.back: Business policies change often (e.g. 'only supervisors see salaries'). Implement the general mechanism; keep the policy as configurable data.
notes.extra: Requirement: 'access only by authorised users'. Policy: who is authorised. Keep them separate.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.front: Why keep a project glossary?
notes.back: So everyone uses the same terms with the same meanings. Teams talking past each other with ambiguous words build the wrong things.
notes.extra: Compare Domain-Driven Design's ubiquitous language.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.front: Feature creep: what's the Pragmatic defence?
notes.back: Make the cost visible: with short iterations and direct client feedback, each extra 'just one more feature' shows up as a trade-off immediately.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.front: What does "Don't think outside the box, find the box" mean?
notes.back: Identify the real constraints. Many assumed constraints are just preconceptions; the real ones define the solution space.
notes.analogy: The Gordian knot: Alexander 'solved' it with his sword because nobody had said the knot must be untied.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.front: Which questions help you when stuck on an "impossible" problem?
notes.back: Is there an easier way? Am I solving the right problem? Why is it a problem? What makes it hard? Must it be done this way, or at all?

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.front: What does "Don't go into the code alone" encourage?
notes.back: Working together: pair programming or mob programming, where several minds catch mistakes, share knowledge and spread ownership.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.front: What does "Agile is not a noun; agile is how you do things" mean?
notes.back: Agility is responding to change with feedback. It can't be bought as a process or tool; adopting rituals isn't the same as being agile.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::08 Before the Project
notes.text: The Pragmatic recipe for agility: work out {{c1::where you are}}; make the {{c2::smallest meaningful step}} towards where you want to be; evaluate {{c3::where you end up}} and fix anything you broke. Repeat.
notes.extra: Apply it at every level: process, team, design and code.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: Why maintain small, stable teams?
notes.back: Stable teams build trust and shared context; small teams communicate easily. The book puts the cap at about 10–12 people.
notes.extra: Tip: Maintain small stable teams.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: Which individual Pragmatic habits must a team adopt as a team?
notes.back: No broken windows, watching for boiled frogs, a shared knowledge portfolio, communication, avoiding duplicated work, and automation.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: What does "Schedule it to make it happen" mean for teams?
notes.back: Improvement work (refactoring, upgrades, learning, experiments) gets done only if it's planned in, not left for spare time.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: What does "Organize fully functional teams" mean?
notes.back: Build teams around end-to-end features (tracer bullets), not technical layers or job functions, so each team can deliver without hand-offs.
notes.extra: Compare stream-aligned teams in Team Topologies.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: What is the lesson of "Coconuts don't cut it"?
notes.back: Copying the visible rituals of successful companies (cargo cult) doesn't copy their results. Context matters.
notes.analogy: Islanders built bamboo airstrips and coconut headphones, but no cargo planes landed.
notes.extra: Tip: Do what works, not what's fashionable.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: What is the Pragmatic goal for delivery cadence?
notes.back: Deliver when users need it. Aim for continuous delivery rather than a fixed, arbitrary release calendar.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.text: The Pragmatic Starter Kit, three foundations for any project: {{c1::version control}}; {{c2::regression testing}}; {{c3::full automation}}.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: What should version control drive?
notes.back: Builds, tests and releases. A commit or tag triggers the pipeline, so releases are repeatable and traceable.
notes.extra: Tip: Use version control to drive builds, tests, and releases.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: When is coding done?
notes.back: When all the tests run. Coding ain't done 'til all the tests run.
notes.extra: Tip: Test early, test often, test automatically.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: What does "Use saboteurs to test your testing" mean?
notes.back: Deliberately introduce bugs and check the tests catch them. Tests that still pass are not protecting you.
notes.extra: Automated form: mutation testing.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: Why test state coverage, not code coverage?
notes.back: Executing every line doesn't test the states the program can be in. 100% line coverage with no edge-case inputs still misses bugs.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: What does "Find bugs once" mean?
notes.back: Once a human finds a bug, it should be the last time a human finds it: add an automated test that catches it from then on.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: What does "Don't use manual procedures" protect against?
notes.back: People aren't repeatable: they forget steps and vary over time. Scripts, pipelines and infrastructure as code do it the same way every time.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: What does "Delight users, don't just deliver code" mean?
notes.back: Your job is to solve the user's business problem, not to complete a feature list. Code is the means, not the outcome.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: Which question helps uncover what users really expect?
notes.back: "How will you know we've all been successful a month (or a year) after this project is done?"
notes.extra: The answers are often business outcomes (e.g. fewer support calls) rather than features.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: Why sign your work?
notes.back: Owning your work publicly makes you proud of it and accountable for it. Anonymity breeds sloppiness and 'not my problem'.
notes.analogy: Medieval stonemasons carved their marks into the stones they cut.

notes.deck: The Pragmatic Programmer::09 Pragmatic Projects
notes.front: What does "First, do no harm" ask of developers?
notes.back: Think about the consequences of your code for users and society. Ask: have I protected the user? Would I use this myself?
notes.extra: Tip: Don't enable scumbags. Refuse to build things that deceive or harm people.
